etymologies.etymologyHTML: A pseudo-Latin form of French compassionné, past participle of compassionner (“feel sorry for”).

definitions.definition: Having, feeling or showing compassion (to or toward someone).

quote.citation: 1611, John Donne, An Anatomy of the World‎[1], London: Samuel Macham:
quote.text: As a compassionate Turcoyse which doth tellBy looking pale, the wearer is not well,

quote.citation: 1675, Robert South, A Sermon preached at Christ-Church, in Twelve Sermons Preached upon Several Occasions, London: Thomas Bennett, 1692, p. 574,[2]
quote.text: […]  there never was any heart truly great and generous, that was not also tender, and compassionate.

quote.citation: 1849 May – 1850 November, Charles Dickens, chapter 49, in The Personal History of David Copperfield, London: Bradbury & Evans, […], published 1850, →OCLC, page 502:
quote.text: He was by nature so exceedingly compassionate of anyone who seemed to be ill at ease  […]  that he shook hands with Mr. Micawber, at least half-a-dozen times in five minutes.

quote.citation: 2007, Mohsin Hamid, chapter 7, in The Reluctant Fundamentalist‎[3], Orlando: Harcourt, page 99:
quote.text: […]  the compassionate pangs I felt for soon-to-be redundant workers were not overwhelming in their frequency; our job required a degree of commitment that left one with rather limited time for such distractions.

definitions.definition: Given to someone as an exception because of a family emergency or a death in their family.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene 3]:
quote.text: It boots thee not to be compassionate:After our sentence plaining comes too late.

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To feel compassion (for someone or with regard to something); to regard (someone or something) with compassion.

quote.citation: 1602, G. Bishop et al., chapter 6, in Thomas Lodge, transl., The Famous and Memorable Workes of Josephus‎[4], London, page 733:
quote.text: […]  seeing them die so wofully in the flames, he compassionated them.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, chapter 6, in The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC, book 2, page 83:
quote.text: The Justice which Mr. Allworthy had executed on Partridge, at first met with universal Approbation; but no sooner had he felt its Consequences, than his Neighbours began to relent, and to compassionate his Case;

quote.citation: 1794, William Godwin, chapter 1, in Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams‎[5], volume 2, London: B. Crosby, page 4:
quote.text: And yet I could not help bitterly compassionating the honest fellow, brought to the gallows, as he was, strictly speaking, by the machinations of that devil incarnate, Mr. Tyrrel.

quote.citation: 1847 October 16, Currer Bell [pseudonym; Charlotte Brontë], chapter III, in Jane Eyre. An Autobiography. […], volume I, London: Smith, Elder, and Co., […], →OCLC, page 38:
quote.text: “ […]  if she were a nice, pretty child, one might compassionate her forlornness; but one really cannot care for such a little toad as that.”

quote.citation: 1848 November – 1850 December, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 16, in The History of Pendennis. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1849–1850, →OCLC:
quote.text: Helen laughed at these sentimental remarks, and wondered that Madame herself did not compassionate her lodger, and console him

quote.citation: 1855, Frederick Douglass, chapter 17, in My Bondage and My Freedom. […], New York, Auburn, N.Y.: Miller, Orton & Mulligan […], →OCLC, part I (Life as a Slave), page 236:
quote.text: I explained the circumstances of the past two days, which had driven me to the woods, and he deeply compassionated my distress.
